review: Draft questions. Not yet reviewed by a pediatric professional.

pre.text: The baby turns toward your hand with an open mouth and brings their fists to their mouth. The last feed started two and a half hours ago. What's a good next step?

options.text: Offer a feed: these can be early hunger cues
Wait until the baby cries, so you know for sure
Lay the baby down for a nap
Offer a little water first

pre.explain: Rooting and hands to the mouth can be early hunger cues. Crying is a late cue, and feeding is easier before it. Babies under 6 months don't need water.

pre.text: During a bottle feed, the baby turns away and closes their mouth. About a third of the bottle is left.

options.text: Encourage them to finish so they sleep longer
Pause, and if they stay turned away, end the feed
Prop the bottle so they can keep sipping
Add cereal to the next bottle

pre.explain: Turning away and closing the mouth can mean full. Let the baby decide how much. Never prop a bottle, and don't add cereal to a bottle unless a clinician says so.

pre.text: The bassinet has a loose blanket and a soft toy in it. What do you do before laying the baby down to sleep?

options.text: Leave the blanket in; it keeps them warm
Lay them on their side so they can see the toy
Remove both, and lay the baby on their back on the firm, flat mattress
Add a pillow to support their head

pre.explain: Every sleep: on the back, alone, in a clear infant sleep space with a firm, flat mattress and a fitted sheet.

pre.text: The baby is still fussy after a feed, a burp and a diaper change, and you feel overwhelmed.

options.text: Keep jiggling harder until the crying stops
Check other possible needs. If you're overwhelmed, lay the baby on their back in a safe crib and take a short break or ask for help
Offer another full feed every time they cry
Leave the baby on the changing table while you rest

pre.explain: Some crying continues even after good care. Never shake a baby. A safe break (baby on their back in a clear crib) and asking for help are good care.

pre.text: Your helper took the 3 AM feed so you could sleep. How should you think about that feed?

options.text: It doesn't count, since you didn't do it
It means the baby needed less care that night
The work still happened. Plan who covers it next time
The helper should only cover emergencies

pre.explain: Covered care is still care. Planning who covers which night wake is part of getting ready.

pre.text: You're about to change a diaper on a changing table. What comes first?

options.text: Lay the baby down, then look for the wipes
Gather the diaper, wipes and clothes first, then keep one hand on the baby
Pull the new diaper up over the umbilical cord stump
Wipe back to front

pre.explain: Supplies first, a hand on the baby on any raised surface, wipe front to back, and fold the diaper below the cord stump.

post.text: Three hours after a feed, the baby is smacking their lips and turning their head side to side with an open mouth.

options.text: These can be hunger cues: check the timing and offer a feed
It's just a reflex, so ignore it until they cry
Start tummy time
Give a little juice

post.explain: Lip smacking and rooting are common early hunger cues. Respond before crying starts. Juice isn't recommended for infants.

post.text: Halfway through a feed, the baby's sucking slows, their hands relax and they push the nipple out.

options.text: Keep offering until the bottle is empty
These can be fullness cues: pause, and end the feed if they stay turned away
Wake them up so they finish
Warm the bottle in the microwave and try again

post.explain: Relaxed hands, slow sucking and pushing the nipple out can mean full. Never microwave a bottle: hot spots can burn.

post.text: The baby fell asleep in your arms on the sofa, and you're getting sleepy too.

options.text: Stay on the sofa; you'll wake up if they move
Lay them on their tummy on the sofa so they sleep longer
Prop them in the car seat on the floor
Lay them on their back in a clear bassinet, or hand off to someone awake

post.explain: Falling asleep with a baby on a sofa or armchair is dangerous. Move them to a safe sleep space on their back, or hand off.

post.text: It's evening and the baby has fussed on and off for an hour, even though they've been fed, changed and burped.

options.text: Assume you're doing something wrong and keep trying new things faster
Try calm holding, rocking or shushing, share the work, and take a safe break if you need one
Feed again every few minutes until they stop
Close the door and leave them crying for the rest of the night

post.explain: Evening fussing is common and can persist after good care. Soothe, share the load and take safe breaks. Ask a clinician about crying that seems unusual.

post.text: You handed off the rest of the night because you were exhausted. What does that show?

options.text: That you failed the trial
That the night was easy
That asking for help is part of good care, and the work still had to be done by someone
That helpers should never be needed

post.explain: Handing off is a safe, responsible choice. Real families plan shifts and ask for help.

post.text: Mid-change, you realize the wipes are across the room.

options.text: Dash over quickly; it only takes a second
Pick the baby up and take them with you
Leave the baby on the table with a toy
Skip cleaning this time

post.explain: Never leave a baby on a raised surface, even for a second. Take them with you, and gather supplies first next time.
